Unit 2 • SL

Programming Fundamentals

Introduction

How do we translate abstract logic into instructions a machine can execute?

This unit focuses on the transition from designed algorithms to executable code. You will learn how to automate logic using programming constructs, exploring how computers store data (variables), manipulate it (operators), repeat it through iteration, and handle errors (exceptions) to build robust software.

You'll start by mastering data types and variables to store information. Then, you'll learn to manipulate text with string operations, build repetition with for and while loops, and finally make your programs reliable using exception handling and debugging techniques.

Variables & Data Storage

A variable is a named location in memory used to store data that can change during execution. Think of it as a labeled box where you can put a value, take it out, or replace it.

  • Declaration: Telling the computer "I need a box named X".
  • Initialization: Putting the first value into that box.
  • Scope: Creating Global variables (visible everywhere) vs Local variables (visible only inside a function).

In Python, variables are dynamically typed, meaning the "box" changes shape to fit the data you put in it (integer, float, string, or boolean).

String Manipulation

Text is stored as Strings — sequences of characters. You'll learn to manipulate them using:

  • Concatenation: Joining strings together (e.g., "Hello" + " " + "World").
  • Slicing: Extracting specific parts of a string (e.g., text[0:3]).
  • Casting: Converting strings to numbers and vice-versa (e.g., int("5")).

Iteration with For and While Loops

Iteration means repeating a block of code. In this unit, you use two loop styles:

  • for loop (count-controlled): best when you know how many repetitions are needed.
  • while loop (condition-controlled): best when repetition should continue until a condition changes.

You will trace loop variables carefully and avoid infinite loops by making sure the loop condition is updated correctly.

Error Handling & Debugging

Programs rarely work perfectly the first time. You will learn to identify and fix three types of errors:

  • Syntax Errors: breaking the rules of the language (like bad grammar).
  • Runtime Errors: crashing during execution (e.g., dividing by zero).
  • Logic Errors: running without crashing but giving the wrong result.

We use try/except blocks to handle Runtime errors gracefully, and trace tables or breakpoints to hunt down Logic errors.

The Golden Rule

"Garbage In, Garbage Out." If your program accepts invalid input, it will produce invalid output. Always validate user input!

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
VariableA designated memory location that stores a value that can change during the execution of a program.
ConstantA value that cannot be altered by the program during normal execution.
IdentifierThe name given to a variable, function, class, or other entity in the code.
DeclarationSpecifying the name and data type of a variable before it is used.
InitializationAssigning an initial value to a variable at the moment it is declared.
ConcatenationThe operation of joining two strings end-to-end.
SlicingExtracting a section (substring) from a string based on proper indices.
ExceptionAn event that disrupts the normal flow of the program's instructions (e.g., DivisionByZero).
DebuggingThe process of identifying and removing errors from computer hardware or software.
BreakpointAn intentional stopping or pausing place in a program, put in place for debugging purposes.

Common Misconceptions

Assignment vs Equality

Confusion between = (assignment: 'make this equal to...') and == (comparison: 'is this equal to...?').

Global vs Local Scope

Believing a variable declared inside a function is accessible everywhere. It dies when the function ends!

Strings are Numbers

Thinking "5" + "5" equals 10. In programming, "5" + "5" equals "55" (concatenation).

Think Deeper

"Why is natural language unsuitable for programming?" Consider the ambiguity of English (e.g., 'I saw the man with the telescope'). Why must code be rigid and unambiguous?
